query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Using an elevated build-plate preheat during the laser-based additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder will enhance microstructural homogenization, reduce thermal gradients, and thereby lower residual stresses, segregation, and defect formation, leading to improved mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi produced via conventional laser powder-bed fusion that typically shows compositional segregation, high residual stresses, and a defect‐rich microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a high build-plate preheat (in the range of approximately 300–600 °C) during the layer deposition step in additive manufacturing.
generation.conditions: Applicable in laser powder-bed fusion processing under inert (argon) atmosphere; the intervention is valid for AlCrFeNiSi as processed with standard powder feedstock and within the preheat temperature range that avoids oxidation or other thermal degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform, homogenized microstructure with minimized elemental segregation and reduced formation of processing defects.
generation.mechanism: Elevated build-plate temperatures lessen the thermal gradients during solidification, which slows the cooling rate. This controlled cooling promotes homogenization of the multi-principal elements, reduces residual thermal stresses, and limits rapid segregation and defect nucleation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, samples produced with elevated preheat are expected to exhibit increased tensile strength and ductility along with lower residual stress and reduced microstructural defects; the effect is directional but the precise quantitative gains remain to be determined.
generation.baseline: Conventional laser powder-bed fusion of AlCrFeNiSi without build-plate preheating, which typically results in more severe segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation.
generation.boundary: Limited to additive manufacturing processing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi using laser powder-bed fusion under controlled inert atmospheres. The hypothesis may not hold for different alloy systems or alternative manufacturing methods where other factors dominate microstructural evolution.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal preheat temperature and its exact impact on residual stress reduction and defect minimization are not precisely quantified; potential risks such as oxidation at high temperatures or deviations in powder behavior remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples via laser powder-bed fusion: one set using the standard process without preheating, and another set using an elevated build-plate preheat (e.g., ~500 °C). Use identical powder feedstock and maintain the same inert atmosphere. Perform microstructural analysis via SEM and EBSD to assess homogeneity and defect density, X-ray diffraction to measure residual stresses, and mechanical tensile tests to compare strength and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated preheat samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in mechanical strength, ductility, lower residual stress, and reduced segregation/defect density relative to the control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . A key component in current tokamak designs is the divertor, which will be in contact with the deuterium-tritium (D-T) plasma and sustain severe fluxes of particles (helium (He) ash, D and T) and heat, along with radiation damage induced by high-energy neutrons [2] , [3] . Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.
